blocks.text: Expectation, written E of X, is the single number that summarizes where a random variable tends to land on average, weighting every possible outcome by how likely it is. It is the mathematical formalization of the everyday idea of an average, but built to account for the fact that some outcomes are more probable than others. This lesson builds directly on the rules covered in the probability rules lesson, and expectation itself becomes the foundation for variance and standard deviation, covered in their own lessons right after this one.

blocks.alt: A random variable's outcomes weighted by probability and summed into an expected value
blocks.caption: Expectation as a probability weighted average

blocks.text: 1. What Expectation Means

Expectation answers the question: if I could repeat this random process an enormous number of times and average the results, what number would I converge toward? It is not the most likely outcome, and it is not necessarily an outcome that can ever actually occur on a single trial.

A classic illustration is a fair six sided die. Each face from 1 to 6 is equally likely, and the expected value of a roll is 3.5, a number that never appears on the die itself. Expectation describes the long run center of mass of the outcomes, not any single realization of them.

The word expectation is a technical term here, distinct from its everyday meaning of anticipating one specific result. In statistics it always refers to this probability weighted average, never to a prediction of what a single trial will produce.
2. The Formula for a Discrete Random Variable

For a discrete random variable X that can take values x1, x2, and so on, expectation is computed as the sum over every possible value of that value times its probability. In words, multiply each outcome by how likely it is, then add up all of those products.

Every term in that sum is an outcome scaled by its probability, and because the probabilities sum to 1 as required by the rules covered in the probability rules lesson, the result is a proper weighted average rather than a plain unweighted one.

The formula works no matter how many distinct values the random variable can take, from a two outcome coin flip to a random variable with thousands of possible categories, as long as every outcome probability is accounted for exactly once in the sum.
3. The Continuous Case, Briefly

When a random variable can take any value in a continuous range rather than a countable list, for example a person's height or a sensor reading, the sum in the discrete formula becomes an integral over the variable's probability density function. The core idea does not change: every possible value is still weighted by how likely it is, the sum operation simply becomes continuous.

code.content:
E[X] = integral over all x of x * f(x) dx
# f(x) is the probability density function of X

blocks.text: The full mechanics of continuous random variables and their density functions are covered in the continuous random variables lesson. For now, the key takeaway is that expectation is defined consistently across both discrete and continuous random variables, only the machinery for combining outcomes changes, covered separately in the discrete random variables and continuous random variables lessons.

One helpful mental shortcut is that the integral in the continuous formula plays exactly the same role as the sum in the discrete formula, both are simply accumulating value times likelihood, just over a continuum instead of a countable list.
4. Expectation as a Weighted Average

An ordinary average treats every data point as equally important. Expectation generalizes that idea by letting each outcome contribute in proportion to its probability. An outcome with probability 0.9 pulls the expected value much closer to it than an outcome with probability 0.01.

Summing the contribution column gives E[X] = 12.0 for this example, even though the most probable single outcome is 0, and the largest possible outcome is 100. Expectation blends both the size and the likelihood of every outcome into one number.

This weighting effect is why rare but extreme outcomes, such as a large financial loss with small probability, can still dominate an expected value calculation even though they almost never occur on any given trial.
5. Linearity of Expectation

Linearity of expectation is one of the most useful facts in all of probability, precisely because it holds unconditionally, no assumption of independence between random variables is required. For any random variables X and Y, and any constants a and b, the expectation of a times X plus b times Y equals a times E[X] plus b times E[Y].

code.content:
E[a*X + b*Y] = a*E[X] + b*E[Y]
# true even if X and Y are dependent on each other

blocks.text: 5.1 Why Independence Is Not Required

This is surprising the first time you see it. Variance, covered in the next lesson, does require care around independence, but expectation does not, because expectation is fundamentally a sum, and sums distribute over addition regardless of how the underlying variables relate to each other.

blocks.title: Worked linearity example
blocks.content: Suppose you roll two fair six sided dice and want the expected value of their sum. Instead of enumerating all 36 outcome pairs, linearity says E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7, computed instantly regardless of the fact that the two dice are independent. The same shortcut still works even for dependent variables, such as X being a die roll and Y being defined as 7 minus X, where E[X + Y] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7 as well.

blocks.text: 6. Expectation of a Constant and of a Function

The expectation of a constant c is simply c itself, since a constant has probability 1 of taking its own value and contributes nothing to be averaged away. This may look trivial, but it becomes an important base case when breaking a complicated expectation into simpler pieces.

Expectation can also be applied to a function of a random variable, written E[g(X)], computed by weighting each value of g(x) by the probability of the underlying x, not by first computing E[X] and then applying g to that number. In general E[g(X)] is not the same as g(E[X]), a distinction that becomes essential once variance, defined as E of a squared deviation, is introduced in the next lesson.

code.content:
# E[g(X)] != g(E[X]) in general
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
probs = np.array([1/3, 1/3, 1/3])
E_x = np.sum(x * probs)
E_x_squared = np.sum((x**2) * probs)
print(E_x**2, E_x_squared)   # 4.0 vs 4.667, not equal

blocks.text: This distinction matters in practice whenever a model output is passed through a nonlinear transformation, such as a sigmoid or an exponential, before its expectation is needed, since the shortcut of applying the function to the mean afterward would silently give the wrong answer.
7. Expectation in Code

Computing expectation directly from a probability mass function is a one line dot product between the outcomes and their probabilities. Libraries such as scipy.stats also expose a mean method for standard distributions, which internally applies the same formula.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

outcomes = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
probs = np.array([1/6]*6)
expected_value = np.dot(outcomes, probs)
print(expected_value)   # 3.5

# using a named distribution
binomial = stats.binom(n=10, p=0.3)
print(binomial.mean())   # 3.0, equals n * p

blocks.text: Sampling based estimation is common in practice too, especially when an exact probability mass function is hard to write down. Drawing a large number of samples and averaging them converges to the true expectation by the law of large numbers.

code.content:
import numpy as np
samples = np.random.binomial(n=10, p=0.3, size=100000)
print(samples.mean())   # close to 3.0 for a large sample size

blocks.text: When working with real datasets rather than a known formula, the sample mean computed by a single call such as numpy mean is itself already an estimate of the expectation, subject to sampling error that shrinks as the dataset grows larger.
8. Expected Loss and Risk in Machine Learning

Nearly every training objective in machine learning is an expectation. A loss function such as cross entropy or mean squared error is first defined for a single example, then the actual quantity a model minimizes is the expected loss across the whole data distribution, approximated in practice by averaging over a training batch.

Empirical risk minimization, the standard framework behind supervised learning, is literally the strategy of minimizing the average loss over a finite training set as a stand in for the true, unknown expected loss over the entire population of possible inputs.

Regularization terms added to a loss function, such as an L2 penalty on the weights, are typically added inside this same expectation, since the full training objective is still, at its core, an expected loss over the data distribution plus a penalty term.
9. Expected Reward in Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning agents are trained to maximize expected cumulative reward, not the reward of any single trajectory. Because an agent environment interaction is stochastic, the same policy can produce different total rewards across different episodes, so the objective is defined as an expectation over the distribution of possible trajectories.

code.content:
# simplified expected return over sampled trajectories
returns = []
for episode in range(num_episodes):
    trajectory_reward = run_episode(policy, environment)
    returns.append(trajectory_reward)
expected_return = sum(returns) / len(returns)   # Monte Carlo estimate of E[Return]

blocks.text: Value functions in reinforcement learning, such as the state value function V(s), are formally defined as the expected return starting from state s, another direct application of the expectation formula covered earlier in this lesson.

The discount factor commonly used in reinforcement learning, which shrinks the weight given to rewards further in the future, is applied inside this same expectation, it does not change the fact that the objective being optimized is still an expected value.
10. Properties That Follow from the Definition

items: Expectation of a constant c equals c.
Expectation is linear: E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y], with no independence assumption needed.
If X is always greater than or equal to Y, then E[X] is greater than or equal to E[Y].
Expectation of the sum equals the sum of expectations, even for a very large number of random variables.
Expectation does not commute with nonlinear functions: E[g(X)] is generally not equal to g(E[X]).

blocks.text: These properties are what make expectation such a convenient building block. Complicated quantities can often be decomposed into sums of simpler random variables, with the total expectation obtained by simply adding up the individual pieces.
11. Law of Large Numbers and Sample Averages

The law of large numbers explains why the sample averages computed in the code examples earlier converge to the true expectation as the number of samples grows. Formally, if X1, X2, and so on are independent draws from the same distribution as X, their running average converges to E[X] as the number of draws goes to infinity.

This is the theoretical justification behind Monte Carlo estimation, used throughout machine learning whenever an exact expectation is intractable to compute in closed form, such as estimating the expected reward of a reinforcement learning policy by averaging over many simulated episodes.

code.content:
import numpy as np

true_mean = 3.5
for n in [10, 1000, 1000000]:
    rolls = np.random.randint(1, 7, size=n)
    print(n, rolls.mean())   # gets closer to 3.5 as n grows

blocks.text: 12. Expectation of Sums of Independent and Identically Distributed Variables

A direct application of linearity is the sum of many independent and identically distributed, or iid, random variables. If X1 through Xn are all draws from the same distribution with expectation mu, the expectation of their sum is simply n times mu, regardless of how large n gets.

This single fact underlies why averaging more data points does not change the expected value of the average itself, only its spread, which is exactly the subject of the variance lesson that follows this one.

code.content:
E[X1 + X2 + ... + Xn] = n * mu
E[(X1 + X2 + ... + Xn) / n] = mu   # the sample mean is itself unbiased

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example

Consider a simplified spam classifier that assigns each incoming email a label, and imagine the classifier is wrong 10 percent of the time, incurring a cost of 5 when it wrongly flags a real email as spam, and a cost of 20 when it wrongly lets a spam email through, with each type of mistake being equally likely among the 10 percent of errors.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Outcome","Probability","Cost","Contribution"],"rows":[["Correct classification","0.90","0","0"],["False positive (real flagged as spam)","0.05","5","0.25"],["False negative (spam let through)","0.05","20","1.0"]]}

blocks.text: Summing the contribution column gives an expected cost of 1.25 per email. This is exactly the kind of calculation that sits behind choosing a classification threshold, minimizing expected cost rather than simply maximizing raw accuracy.

Notice that the expected cost calculation here mirrors exactly the weighted average table shown earlier in this lesson, only the labels have changed from abstract outcomes to concrete classifier mistakes.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Treating the expected value as a value the random variable must actually be able to take, when it is frequently a number that never occurs on any single trial, such as 3.5 for a die roll.
Assuming E[g(X)] equals g(E[X]) for a nonlinear function g, when in general it does not.
Forgetting that linearity of expectation holds even when the underlying random variables are dependent, and reaching for a more complicated calculation than necessary.
Confusing expectation, a single summary number, with the full probability distribution, which contains far more information than the average alone.
Computing an average over observed samples and treating it as the exact expectation, rather than as an estimate that carries its own sampling uncertainty.

blocks.title: A concrete instance of the E[g(X)] mistake
blocks.content: Suppose X is the number of daily active users of an app, uncertain but averaging E[X] = 1000, and a business wants the expected value of revenue defined as X squared times a constant, because of network effects. Plugging the average number of users into the formula and squaring it gives a wrong answer, since E[X squared] is not equal to E[X] squared unless X has zero variance, a case covered in the next lesson.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Compute Expectation in Code

Try the following exercise. A biased coin comes up heads with probability 0.3 and tails with probability 0.7. Define heads as the value 1 and tails as the value 0, then compute the expected value both by hand using the formula and by simulation.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# by hand
outcomes = np.array([1, 0])
probs = np.array([0.3, 0.7])
expected_by_formula = np.dot(outcomes, probs)
print(expected_by_formula)   # should print 0.3

# by simulation
flips = np.random.binomial(n=1, p=0.3, size=200000)
print(flips.mean())   # should be close to 0.3

blocks.text: Notice that the expected value of a coin defined this way, 0.3, is exactly the probability of heads. This is a general fact worth remembering: for any indicator variable that is 1 on some event and 0 otherwise, the expectation of that indicator equals the probability of the event.

As a follow up exercise, try changing the coin bias to 0.65 and confirm that both the formula based calculation and the simulation based estimate converge to 0.65, reinforcing that the expectation of an indicator variable always equals the probability of the event it indicates.
Key Takeaway

Expectation compresses an entire probability distribution into a single number by weighting every possible outcome by how likely it is, generalizing the everyday notion of an average into something that respects unequal likelihoods. Its defining formula differs between discrete and continuous random variables, but its meaning, a probability weighted center of mass, stays exactly the same across both.

Linearity of expectation, holding regardless of dependence between variables, makes expectation one of the most tractable tools in probability, and it shows up constantly in AI systems, from the expected loss a model minimizes during training to the expected reward a reinforcement learning agent tries to maximize. The next lesson builds directly on top of this idea, defining variance as the expected squared deviation from this very expectation.
